summary: Deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategies: cache keys, hit rate expectations, multi-tenant safety, eviction and TTL policies, warmup strategies, and how caching interacts with batching and quantization. Customer is evaluating hosted vs private (VPC/on-prem) with strict security requirements and wants realistic hit rates and failure modes for a production rollout.
transcript:
[00:00] Avery (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro: I'm Avery, AE. Ravi is our SE; Lina on solutions. Maya, Carlos, Priya, Tom from Sierra?
[00:10] Maya (Sierra): Yep hi all, thanks. we are mostly focused on reducing token cost while keeping latency under 200ms p50 for our chat endpoint. happy to dive in.
[00:22] Ravi (Redwood): Great. goal for today: walk through prefix / prompt caching options (keys, sharding, TTLs), expected hit rates with your workload, and caveats for multi-tenant environments and VPC/on-prem deployments.
[00:36] Carlos (Sierra): Quick context: we have a multi-tenant product with 120 tenants, 8 models in rotation, and average prompt length ~120 tokens, some long histories to 2k tokens. We run both synchronous chat and async batch summarization.
[00:52] Priya (Sierra): security note: we need encryption at rest for cached payloads, and audits for any persisted context. SOC2 is required.
[01:03] Ravi: Understood. Redwood supports KMS-backed encryption for cache stores and audit logging; in private deployments you control the KMS keys. We'll include the security doc.
[01:18] Tom (Sierra): timeline: PoC in 2–3 weeks, then pilot. We need realistic numbers for hit rate to justify cost savings.
[01:27] Avery: ok good. let's jump into cache key design.
[01:32] [01:32] Ravi: the naive key is full prompt hash, but with dynamic system prompts and per-tenant personalization that yields low reuse. We see better results with prefix-based keys: hash of static system prompt + last N user tokens or embedding of the prefix. That gives higher hit-rate for assistant-stable prefixes.
[01:50] Maya: so we should include tenant id in the key? we worry about cross-tenant leaks.
[01:57] Ravi: Yes, include tenant id and model version in cache key. Multi-tenant safety best practices: tenant-scoped caches (key prefixing) or namespace-isolated shards. For hosted multi-tenant you must ensure plaintext cache contents cannot be read by other tenants; we encrypt and namespace. For private installs, you can mount a per-tenant cache store.
[02:21] Carlos: curious about memory sizing: if we shard per-tenant, we might waste memory. any guidance?
[02:27] Ravi: common pattern: global cache with tenant prefix + per-tenant quotas and eviction weights. For a small number of tenants, per-tenant shards make sense; at 120 tenants, a single store with strong eviction policies and per-tenant counters is more memory efficient. We can expose metrics per-tenant to avoid noisy tenants dominating.
[02:45] [02:45] Maya: hit-rate expectations — what do you normally see?
[02:49] Ravi: depends on prompt stability. For product prompts that are mostly system instructions + a short user prompt (<= 40 tokens), hit rates can be 30–60% on chat workloads. For long conversational histories and unique user text, hit rates drop to single digits. With prefix canonicalization and normalization (strip timestamps, user ids), we saw improvements from ~8% to ~35% in pilots.
[03:12] Maya: how do you canonicalize safely without removing user-specific info that changes output?
[03:17] Ravi: heuristic: only normalize stable system parts and strip high-entropy tokens (timestamps, session ids). Use template matching for known fields. Also we suggest tuning the prefix window size: last 20–40 tokens is often a good balance.
[03:31] [03:31] Priya: what about privacy/regulatory — do we persist PII in cache?
[03:36] Ravi: by default, redact sensitive entities before caching or use ephemeral caches (in-memory TTL < few seconds) for inputs flagged as PII. For enterprise/private, a policy plugin can prevent caching of any prompts with PII markers. We'll share detection heuristics.
[03:50] Tom: eviction and TTL strategies?
[03:53] Ravi: hybrid approach: TTL + LRU with weighted eviction by tenant. TTL can be shorter for dynamic prompts, longer for stable system prompts. Example: system prompt cache 24h, user prompt fragment 5–30 min depending on reuse. Also a stale-while-revalidate model helps: serve stale cached responses while recomputing in background to keep latency low.
[04:13] [04:13] Carlos: how does caching interact with KV cache inside the model runtime (i.e., per-token KV cache)?
[04:20] Ravi: important distinction: prefix/prompt cache stores completed model outputs for a given prompt key (so you can return tokens without invoking the model). The model KV cache is runtime state used during generation to avoid recomputing attention. When using partial results or streaming, we can rehydrate the model's KV cache from saved checkpoints for that prefix, which is an advanced pattern. That's heavier but gives lower generation time for long prefixes. We support both returning full cached output and rehydrating KV state for fast continuation.
[04:46] Maya: rehydrating KV cache sounds great but is that portable across model versions or quantization variants?
[04:52] Ravi: KV caches are model-architecture and quantization specific. You must include model binary version and quantization profile in the cache key. Rehydration across major model updates is brittle. For safe rollouts, we fallback to full recompute when mismatch detected.
[05:07] [05:07] Priya: encryption at rest for cached KV state? any perf impact?
[05:12] Ravi: encrypting cache blobs with KMS adds minimal CPU overhead on read/write if you use envelope encryption. For high-throughput stores we recommend local node-level disk encryption with KMS for key rotation; for hosted we manage that.
[05:25] Tom: batching interaction: if we enable aggressive batching for throughput, does that reduce cache hitability?
[05:31] Ravi: batching is orthogonal but interacts with latency SLOs. Caching reduces backend load, which can increase effective batch sizes on remaining requests. However, careful: if you serve cached responses from a fast in-memory path, those requests don't enter batchers; that skews batching statistics. In practice caching lowers cost and increases throughput headroom.
[05:50] [05:50] Carlos: quantization — any effects on cached outputs? are outputs stable when switching from fp16 to 8-bit quant?
[05:57] Ravi: quantization can slightly change token probabilities leading to different continuation tokens in marginal cases. So cache keys should include quantization/precision profile. For deterministic models and nucleus sampling with fixed seed, outputs can be stable, but we recommend conservative validation: run A/B on a subset to ensure quality preserved.
[06:16] Maya: hit-rate simulator — what inputs do you need?
[06:19] Ravi: representative prompt corpus (we only need samples, not full PII), distribution of sequence lengths, counts by tenant, and your system prompt variants. We'll run a simulated pass with various prefix window sizes and canonicalization heuristics.
[06:30] [06:30] Priya: VPC/on-prem constraints: what differs?
[06:33] Ravi: main differences: you control the cache store (Redis/rocksdb), encryption, and network egress. For on-prem, we recommend co-locating cache stores with serving nodes to minimize network hops. For VPC, ensure subnet placement and security groups allow high-throughput links. Also private deploys can mount local SSD-backed stores for KV rehydration—much faster than networked caches.
[06:56] Carlos: failure modes — stale or inconsistent caches under rollouts?
[07:00] Ravi: yes. common failure modes: serving stale outputs after model changes, cross-tenant key collisions, and cache storms on cold starts. Mitigations: include model_version+quant profile in keys, atomically invalidate during rollouts, use randomized warmup to avoid stampedes, and rate-limit recompute paths. Also expose metrics: per-key TTL, per-tenant hit/miss counters, and rehydrate-failure rates.
[07:26] [07:26] Tom: example numbers?
[07:28] Ravi: in one e-comm customer, prefix caching reduced tokens by 42% and cut per-request GPU time 33%, with avg latency improving by ~40ms p50. But results vary. We'll provide a benchmarking template.
[07:45] Maya: what about legal — logs, audit trail for cache hits?
[07:49] Ravi: we can log hit events with masked keys, or log only metrics aggregated by tenant. For SOC2 we provide audit logs showing who purged caches and when. Private deployments let you keep full audit trails internally.
[08:02] [08:02] Carlos: how to handle dynamic system prompts that change often (A/B tests)?
[08:07] Ravi: treat experiment variants as part of cache key. Use short TTLs for variant-driven prompts. When you flip an experiment, do an atomic cache invalidation for affected namespaces.
[08:19] Maya: are there built-in Redwood policies for PII redaction before caching?
[08:24] Lina (Redwood): yes we have a policy engine that can run regex/entity detectors and tag blobs as non-cacheable or redact them. We can ship a default config and tune.
[08:35] [08:35] Priya: performance profiler — we need traces that show time spent in cache lookup vs model vs batching.
[08:41] Ravi: Redwood Console exposes per-route breakdowns: cache lookup latency, backend generation, batching delay, and network. We'll share a demo dashboard and the tracing hook to correlate traces with your app traces.
[08:55] Carlos: multi-tenant noisy neighbor — curious about throttling.
[08:59] Ravi: per-tenant rate limits and token budgets plus weighted LRU eviction help. Also we surface per-tenant cost by token so ops can throttle heavy tenants before they impact others.
[09:12] [09:12] Tom: any gotchas for rehydration at scale?
[09:16] Ravi: rehydration requires serializing KV caches; they can be large for long prefixes. Use chunking and compressing, and only rehydrate for high-value prefixes. Also pre-warm commonly used rehydration blobs on node startup.
[09:30] Maya: okay great. what's our recommended initial config for the PoC?
[09:34] Ravi: start with: tenant-scoped keys (tenant_id + model_version + prefix_hash), prefix window 30 tokens, canonicalize system prompts only, TTLs: 30 min user fragments / 24h system fragments, monitor per-tenant hit/miss and latency, and enable stale-while-revalidate for p50 SLA. For private/VPC use local SSD-backed store for rehydration trials.
[09:58] [09:58] Priya: security checklist for PoC?
[10:02] Lina: we'll send SOC2 + KMS docs, and a private-deploy checklist: network, KMS, audit log endpoints, and PII redaction config.
[10:13] Avery: Recap and next steps?
[10:16] Ravi: we'll run a hit-rate simulator once Sierra sends the sample prompt corpus. We'll include quantization variants in keys and produce an estimate of token savings.
[10:25] Maya: i'll send samples by Friday and set up the pilot environment.
[10:29] Tom: we'll unblock infra notes to Carlos.
[10:32] Priya: we'll review the SOC doc once it's shared.
[10:35] Avery: awesome. we'll follow up with the design doc and schedule the on-prem benchmark. Thanks everyone.
[10:40] Maya: thanks all.
[10:42] [END]
